Positionen und Begriffe, p. 113, note — PuB, p. 128, note 2.
It lives on as a ghost … — See the note above on p. 207.
They have Niehans-style fresh cells injected into themselves — This refers to Pope Pius XII; see above, p. 297.
see Lucan (sed victa Catoni) — Pharsalia, I, 128; see also the note above on p. 79.
Henri Lévy-Bruhl — H. Lévy-Bruhl (1884–1964), sociologist of law and professor of Roman law at the University of Paris.
Pascal’s “human condition” (fr. 139) — Schmitt is using Brunschvicg’s numbering. The fragment says:
“all the unhappiness of men comes from one thing: their inability to remain quietly alone in their room.”
B. Pascal, Über die Religion und über einige andere Gegenstände (Pensées). Translated and edited by Ewald Wasmuth, 8th ed., Heidelberg 1978, p. 77.
Hobbes’s sociology of competition — Schmitt is referring to Chapter 13 of Leviathan.
pp. 511/12 PhdG — See G. W. F. Hegel, Werke. Edited by Eva Moldenhauer and Karl Markus Michel, vol. 3, p. 571.
Mr. von Sedlmayer — Hans Sedlmayr, Verlust der Mitte. Die bildende Kunst des 19. und 20. Jahrh. als Symbol der Zeit, Salzburg 1948.
Ernst Bloch: the fascist Carl Schmitt … —

“The way the universal plays with individuals is called here not only cunning but mystification or cheating […] This is a final echo of the capitalist complex of cunning, which, not without reason—namely, in complete harmony with every reactionary fraud—the fascist Carl Schmitt was the first to point out […]”
E. Bloch, Subjekt – Objekt. Erläuterungen zu Hegel. Expanded edition, Frankfurt am Main 1971, pp. 235 f.
According to Günter Maschke, Bloch said during a lecture in 1965:
“That dog Carl Schmitt—I repeat: that dog Carl Schmitt.”

Ernst Bloch (1885–1977), whom Schmitt probably knew from their shared work for the journal Summa, had still written positively before 1933 about the author of Political Romanticism; see BW Feuchtwanger, p. 35.
In a diary entry of 8 May 1945, Schmitt wrote of Bloch:

“First, in 1917 in Munich at the General Command, his book Spirit of Utopia. Then I saw him at Feuchtwanger’s. He spoke about my Political Romanticism and saw everything accurately, including the fact that I am a born victim for literary plunder.”

and is made a professor for it — In 1948, Bloch, then sixty-four years old, was offered the chair of philosophy in Leipzig. Against the resistance of the faculty, the Ministry of Public Education installed him as professor and director of the Institute of Philosophy.
my copy into the hands of Karl Löwith — See M. Tielke, “Die Bibliothek Carl Schmitts.” In: Schmittiana NF I, 2011, p. 269.
taedium fugae — “weariness of flight”; see Schmitt’s letter to E. Jünger of 11 June 1948:
“I suffer from taedium fugae, and I am heartily tired of the hunt whose quarry I have now been for years.”
Évidemment, ce ne sont pas seulement nos actes qui nous suivent — “Obviously, it is not only our actions that follow us.” See the note above on p. 202.
Unwillingly and only faithfully — See the note above on p. 19.
I am terrified by my power … — From Arthur Schnitzler, Der Puppenspieler. In: idem, Gesammelte Werke, section II, vol. 3, Berlin 1922, p. 267.
Great Wurstel — Zum großen Wurstel, a play by Arthur Schnitzler.
Joh. Adams — Johannes Adams, son of Alfons Adams; see above, p. 325.

L. Ilschner — Author of the following book: Liselotte Ilschner, Rembrandt als Erzieher und seine Bedeutung. Studie über d. kulturelle Struktur d. neunziger Jahre, Danzig [1928]. Ilschner also worked on Shakespeare; four of her letters survive in Schmitt’s papers.
Germany is Hamlet — Quotation from Ferdinand Freiligrath’s 1848 poem “Hamlet”; see C. Schmitt, Hamlet oder Hekuba. Der Einbruch der Zeit in das Spiel, 2nd ed., Stuttgart 1993, p. 11.
Heller’s interjection — See the note above on p. 274.
E. Jünger counts himself among the Order of the Shandians —
“And so, under worthy circumstances, I entered the secret Order of the Shandians, to which I have remained faithful to this day.”
E. Jünger, Sämtliche Werke, vol. 9, p. 38. This refers to Laurence Sterne’s The Life and Opinions of Tristram Shandy, Gentleman.

Rameau’s Nephew — The nephew of Jean-Philippe Rameau, composer and author of an influential theory of harmony, was the failed artist Jean-François Rameau. Denis Diderot’s posthumous work Le neveu de Rameau was translated into German by Goethe in 1805 and published for the first time in that translation.
as Kommerell says — Max Kommerell, Lessing und Aristoteles. Unters. über die Theorie der Tragödie, Frankfurt am Main 1984, p. 32.
parable of the forged rings — See Carl Schmitt, “Die vollendete Reformation. Zu neuen Leviathan-Interpretationen.” In: Leviathan, p. [163].

Habermas at the conference of the “Bund” — A conference entitled “Kulturkonsum und Konsumkultur” was held in Wuppertal in 1955, at which Jürgen Habermas discussed with Arnold Gehlen and Günther Anders; see Bericht über die Tagung „Kulturkonsum und Konsumkultur“, Wuppertal 1955.
I had jokingly defined — Schmitt probably means his preface to the second edition of Political Romanticism, where he writes:

“For what has art meant socially since Romanticism? Either it ended in l’art pour l’art, in the polarity between snobbery and bohemia, or it became a matter of private producers of art supplying private consumers interested in art.”
threw me into what they called automatic arrest — Incorrect; see the note above on p. 201.
Why don’t you ask Mr. Kranzbühler — Otto Kranzbühler (1907–2004), naval judge, defense counsel for Dönitz and Flick at the Nuremberg trials.
the conversation with Nicolaus — N. Sombart. Nothing more can be established about this conversation, but on 20 June 1973 Schmitt wrote to N. Sombart:
“I would very much like to know what you think of the ‘Lincolnization’ of Benito Cereno carried out by Marianne Kesting—now a professor in Bielefeld.”
Listen and suffer — See the note above on p. 227.
“Then, against that overwhelming superiority in armament, another technical means was discovered—gunpowder. Humanity needed it, and immediately it was there.”
G. F. W. Hegel, Vorlesungen über die Philosophie der Geschichte. In: idem, Werke. Edited by Moldenhauer and Michel, vol. 12, Frankfurt am Main 1970, p. 481. See Nomos, p. 299.

lecture by Kojève — Alexandre Kojève (1902–1968), Russian philosopher and Hegel scholar, gave a lecture to the Rhine-Ruhr Club in Düsseldorf on 16 January 1957 entitled “Kolonialismus in europäischer Sicht” (“Colonialism from a European Perspective”). See Schmittiana VI, 1998, which also prints the text of the lecture and the incomplete correspondence between Schmitt and Kojève.

Konrad Kaletsch told me about the incident … — K. Kaletsch (1898–1978), cousin of Friedrich Flick and, from 1924 onward, a member of the Flick Group’s executive board, ultimately as a personally liable partner. He had known Schmitt since the summer of 1945, when he commissioned an expert opinion from Schmitt concerning Flick; see Angriffskrieg, pp. 127 ff.

Kaletsch was charged at Nuremberg together with Friedrich Flick but was acquitted. While Flick was imprisoned, Kaletsch conducted negotiations with the Allies over plans for seizure and liquidation. The Maxhütte works, which belonged to the Flick Group, were initially partly expropriated after 1945. After long negotiations, Flick recovered full ownership in 1955; see Norbert Frei, Flick. Der Konzern, die Familie, die Macht, Munich 2009, pp. 478–504.
The “incident” was described in Der Spiegel on 27 January 1957:

“The ceremonial reception given by the Bavarian state government at the end of an inspection tour by the investment committee of the Coal and Steel Community Parliament, at Nuremberg’s Grand Hotel, was marred by a protocol blunder. Before dinner, the French delegate—former Minister of Justice and current Popular Republican member of the French National Assembly, Professor de Menthon—refused to take the seat assigned to him beside the industrial magnate Friedrich Flick. Shortly before, the committee had visited Flick’s major Bavarian plant, the Maximilianshütte in Sulzbach-Rosenberg. Bavarian Economics Minister Bezold (FDP) tried in vain to talk Professor de Menthon out of his resentment toward Flick, who had been the principal defendant in the Nuremberg trial named after him. In the end, the Frenchman exchanged seats with a German colleague on the committee. De Menthon had served as the chief French prosecutor at the International Military Tribunal in Nuremberg.”

François de Menthon (1900–1984) was the chief French prosecutor at the Nuremberg trials. Jean Armengaud, French general, had been air attaché in Warsaw in 1939 and appeared as a witness at the Nuremberg trials.
in my essay “Die Buribunken” — In: Summa, 1918, 4, pp. 89–106; reprinted in Tb 1915, pp. 453–471.

Kojève avoided … every reference to current affairs — The following paragraphs are largely identical to Schmitt’s letter to Nicolaus Sombart of 3 February 1957 (BW Sombart, pp. 96 ff.). Sombart had intended to attend Kojève’s lecture but cancelled at the last moment.

the chapter “Plotnoi” in Mutius’s Katorgan — Bernhard von Mutius (1913–1979), Schmitt’s assistant at Berlin University in 1934/35. From 1949 he worked in the East German Foreign Ministry. In 1950 he was arrested for espionage and sentenced to forced labor in Vorkuta. In 1955 he was released as part of the freeing of German prisoners of war secured by Adenauer.

Under a pseudonym he published a book about his time in the Soviet labor camp: Bernhard Roeder, Der Katorgan, Cologne/Berlin 1956; the chapter “Der Plotnoi” appears on pp. 83–98. A presentation copy is in Schmitt’s papers, RW 265 no. 26443.
Schmitt wrote to Forsthoff on 15 February 1956:
“Mutius … is coming tomorrow for a few days.”

Mutius is also discussed at length in Schmitt’s letters to N. Sombart, who had known him since the early 1930s and later became his colleague and friend at the Council of Europe in Strasbourg. In 1979 Sombart delivered the funeral address for him; typescript in Schmitt’s papers, RW 265 no. 21820.

Nicolaus asked about the patriot — See Nicolaus Sombart, “Patriotismus im Welt-Bürgerkrieg.” In: Der Zeitgenosse und sein Vaterland. Eine Vortragsreihe des Bayerischen Rundfunks. Edited by Gerhard Szczesny, Munich 1957, pp. 31–51.
I answered him — Letter of 3 February 1957 (BW Sombart, pp. 96 ff.).
“Those were never your bells …” — From the poem “Venus Religio” by Richard Dehmel (1863–1920), in: R. Dehmel, Die Verwandlung der Venus, Berlin 1907, p. 59.
Peter Schneider’s book — See the note above on p. 329.
πολλὰ τὰ δεινά — πολλὰ τὰ δεινά κοὐδὲν ἀνθρώπου δεινότερον πέλει.
“Many powerful things exist, but nothing is more powerful than man.”
